entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14089"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.11.1-Mark.11.11">Mr 11:1-11</reference>. Christ's Triumphal Entry into Jerusalem, on the First Day of the Week. ( = <reference osisRef="Matt.21.1-Matt.21.9">Mt 21:1-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.19.29-Luke.19.40">Lu 19:29-40</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.12">Joh 12:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.12.19">19</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen27195" type="x-p"/> See on <reference osisRef="Luke.19.29-Luke.19.40">Lu 19:29-40</reference>.<div eID="gen27195" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.11.11-Mark.11.26">Mr 11:11-26</reference>. The Barren Fig Tree Cursed with Lessons from It--Second Cleansing of the Temple, on the Second and Third Days of the Week. ( =</title> <div sID="gen27196" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Matt.21.12-Matt.21.22">Mt 21:12-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.19.45-Luke.19.48">Lu 19:45-48</reference>).<div eID="gen27196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27197" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14089"/><hi type="bold">11. And Jesus entered into Jerusalem, and into the temple: and when he had looked round about upon--</hi>surveyed.<div eID="gen27197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27198" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all things, and now the eventide was come, he went out into Bethany with the twelve--</hi>Thus briefly does our Evangelist dispose of this His first day in Jerusalem, after the triumphal entry. Nor do the Third and Fourth Gospels give us more light. But from Matthew (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.10">Mt 21:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.14-Matt.11.16">11, 14-16</reference>) we learn some additional and precious particulars, for which see on <reference osisRef="Luke.19.45-Luke.19.48">Lu 19:45-48</reference>. entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 11 Mr 11:1-11 . Christ's Triumphal Entry into Jerusalem, on the First Day of the Week. ( = Mt 21:1-9 ; Lu 19:29-40 ; Joh 12:12 , 19 ). See on Lu 19:29-40 . Mr 11:11-26 . The Barren Fig Tree Cursed with Lessons from It--Second Cleansing of the Temple, on the Second and Third Days of the Week. ( = Mt 21:12-22 ; Lu 19:45-48 ). 11. And Jesus entered into Jerusalem, and into the temple: and when he had looked round about upon-- surveyed. all things, and now the eventide was come, he went out into Bethany with the twelve-- Thus briefly does our Evangelist dispose of this His first day in Jerusalem, after the triumphal entry. Nor do the Third and Fourth Gospels give us more light. But from Matthew ( Mt 21:10 , 11, 14-16 ) we learn some additional and precious particulars, for which see on Lu 19:45-48 . It was not now safe for the Lord to sleep in the city, nor, from the day of His Triumphal Entry, did He pass one night in it, save the last fatal one. The Barren Fig Tree Cursed ( Mr 11:12-14 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14090"/><div sID="gen27200" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14090"/><hi type="bold">12. And on the morrow--</hi>The Triumphal Entry being on the first day of the week, this following day was Monday.<div eID="gen27200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27201" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when they were come from Bethany--</hi>"in the morning" (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.18">Mt 21:18</reference>).<div eID="gen27201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27202" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he was hungry--</hi>How was that? Had he stolen forth from that dear roof at Bethany to the "mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer to God?" (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.12">Lu 6:12</reference>); or, "in the morning," as on a former occasion, "risen up a great while before day, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed" (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.35">Mr 1:35</reference>); not breaking His fast thereafter, but bending His steps straight for the city, that He might "work the works of Him that sent Him while it was day?" (<reference osisRef="John.9.4">Joh 9:4</reference>). We know not, though one lingers upon and loves to trace out the every movement of that life of wonders. One thing, however we are sure of--it was real bodily hunger which He now sought to allay by the fruit of this fig tree, "if haply He might find any thing thereon"; not a mere scene for the purpose of teaching a lesson, as some early heretics maintained, and some still seem virtually to hold. <div eID="gen27202" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14091"/><div sID="gen27203" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14091"/><hi type="bold">13. And seeing a fig tree--</hi>(In <reference osisRef="Matt.21.19">Mt 21:19</reference>, it is "one fig tree," but the sense is the same as here, "a certain fig tree," as in <reference osisRef="Matt.8.19">Mt 8:19</reference>, &c.). Bethphage, which adjoined Bethany, derives its name from its being a fig region--"House of figs."<div eID="gen27203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27204" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">afar off having leaves--</hi>and therefore promising fruit, which in the case of figs come before the leaves.<div eID="gen27204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27205" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he came, if haply he might find any thing thereon: and when he came to it, he found nothing but leaves; for the time of figs was not yet--</hi>What the precise import of this explanation is, interpreters are not agreed. Perhaps all that is meant is, that as the proper fig season had not arrived, no fruit would have been expected even of this tree but for the leaves which it had, which were in this case prematurely and unnaturally developed. <div eID="gen27205" type="x-p"/>

Perhaps all that is meant is, that as the proper fig season had not arrived, no fruit would have been expected even of this tree but for the leaves which it had, which were in this case prematurely and unnaturally developed.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14093"/><div sID="gen27211" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14093"/><hi type="bold">20. And in the morning--</hi>of Tuesday, the third day of the week: He had slept, as during all this week, at Bethany.<div eID="gen27211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27212" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as they passed by--</hi>going into Jerusalem again.<div eID="gen27212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27213" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they saw the fig tree dried up from the roots--</hi>no partial blight, leaving life in the root; but it was now dead, root and branch. In <reference osisRef="Matt.21.19">Mt 21:19</reference> it is said it withered away as soon as it was cursed. But the full blight had not appeared probably at once; and in the dusk perhaps, as they returned to Bethany, they had not observed it. The precision with which Mark distinguishes the days is not observed by Matthew, intent only on holding up the truths which the incident was designed to teach. In Matthew the whole is represented as taking place at once, just as the two stages of Jairus' daughter--dying and dead--are represented by him as one. The only difference is between a more summary and a more detailed narrative, each of which only confirms the other. <div eID="gen27213" type="x-p"/>

Matthew ( Mt 21:20 ) gives this simply as a general exclamation of surprise by the disciples "how soon" the blight had taken effect.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14096"/><div sID="gen27217" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14096"/><hi type="bold">23. For verily I say unto you, That whosoever shall say unto this mountain, Be thou removed ... he shall have whatsoever he saith--</hi>Here is the lesson now. From the nature of the case supposed--that they might wish a mountain removed and cast into the sea, a thing far removed from anything which they could be thought actually to desire--it is plain that not physical but moral obstacles to the progress of His kingdom were in the Redeemer's view, and that what He designed to teach was the great lesson, that no obstacle should be able to stand before a confiding faith in God. <div eID="gen27217" type="x-p"/>
